absent: Numeric trap vectors, error-code format, and register layout of pt_regs beyond field names used.
Semantics of common reporters and terminators such as error-trap, trap delivery, die, panic, and notifier return codes.
Encoding and length rules for bug traps, instruction decoder details, and address-reference resolution.
User split-lock, UMIP, vDSO, vsyscall, virtual-8086, kprobe, KGDB, and text-poke handler contracts.
Full user-mode debug event delivery and signal generation after notifier consumption.
Locking beyond interrupt enable and disable and nonmaskable entry and exit pairing.

findings.text: Invalid-opcode vector first attempts kernel bug-trap emulation before formal exception entry to avoid recursion, and otherwise establishes exception entry state, reports an invalid opcode fault, then exits exception state.

Kernel bug emulation decodes the trapping instruction at the saved program counter, dispatches warn versus fatal families through reporting helpers, restores interrupt enable according to saved flags, advances past the trapping instruction only when handled and otherwise restores the original counter.

Coprocessor overrun, invalid task-state segment, segment-not-present and stack-segment vectors all funnel into a common error-trap reporter with distinct trap numbers and signals, carrying the hardware error code except for the overrun case.

Alignment-check vector offers a die-chain notifier first, treats kernel mode as fatal split-lock, enables interrupts for user handling, attempts user split-lock recovery, otherwise delivers a bus fault, then disables interrupts before return.

Stack-guard violation handling is terminal: it announces the stack kind and fault versus stack bounds, invokes fatal exception termination, then panics if termination ever returned, so callers never resume.

Double-fault handling special-cases a failing return-to-user frame on the fixup stack by rebuilding a general-protection frame on the normal entry stack and redirecting to that vector; otherwise it uses nonmaskable entry, notifies the die chain, records trap state on the thread, checks whether the saved fault address lies in a guard page to delegate to stack-overflow handling, then reports and terminates fatally.
Bounds vector offers die-chain notification first, conditionally enables interrupts, treats kernel mode as fatal, delivers a segmentation fault to user mode, then conditionally disables interrupts.

Kernel general-protection diagnostics classify the suspected address into no hint, canonical kernel address, noncanonical address, separation violation, or null-pointer style low address, each with a short human explanation used in the fault message.

General-protection address inference safely copies the faulting instruction bytes, decodes them in kernel mode, resolves the referenced memory operand against saved registers, rejects unresolvable references, and applies canonical-half and feature checks to select a hint.

Privilege-flag emulation only applies where the feature is built and the thread requests full emulation; it reads one user byte at the effective instruction pointer, swallows only interrupt-flag opcodes, emits a rate-limited one-time warning, and advances the program counter by one byte.

General-protection dispatch prefers a user PASID activation fix with interrupts disabled, redirects virtual-8086 mode to its fault handler, tries ordered user recoveries for privilege-flag emulation, vector-DSO, user-instruction protection and legacy system-call emulation before forcing a segmentation fault, and for kernel mode tries exception fixup plus probe and die-chain handling before emitting an enriched fatal report.

Breakpoint vector first handles text-poke breakpoints without further calls, then splits by privilege: user mode uses user exception entry and exit around trap delivery, while kernel mode uses nonmaskable entry and terminates fatally when debugger, probe and die-chain consumers decline.

Entry helpers normalize register frames: one synchronizes an entry frame onto the top of the current stack, one relocates a vectoring frame off an interrupt stack onto a safe stack, and one rebuilds a corrupted return-to-user frame onto the task entry stack while asserting a user target.

Off-interrupt-stack switching distrusts the stack pointer inside the system-call gap and uses the current stack top, otherwise validates the supplied stack and falls back to a dedicated vectoring stack for entry or unknown kinds, then copies the register frame to an aligned location.

Bad return-to-user recovery copies the five-word return target from the faulty stack into temporary storage, copies the remaining registers from the faulty frame, writes the merged frame onto the task entry stack, and requires the rebuilt frame to indicate user mode.

Debug status handling reads the status register, flips reserved polarity, immediately rewrites the architectural reset value, filters single-step traps inside the system-call entry region when flexible return is absent, and for kernel mode saves debug control, uses nonmaskable entry, re-arms branch-trace flag when requested, offers notifier consumption, and warns while clearing a stray single-step flag.

Fault vectors manage interrupts explicitly: alignment handling enables then disables around user recovery, while bounds, breakpoint and general-protection paths use conditional enable on entry and matching conditional disable on exit, with nonmaskable entry for kernel breakpoint, debug and double-fault contexts.

Vectors map to signals as observed facts: invalid opcode to illegal instruction, coprocessor overrun to floating-point exception, invalid task-state fault to segmentation fault, segment and stack faults plus alignment faults to bus error with alignment detail for the latter, double fault and bounds and general protection to segmentation fault, breakpoint and debug to trap.
Double fault after notification and optional stack-overflow delegation always proceeds to fatal termination and halt, never returning to the interrupted context.
A tiny predicate helper always reports true, provided both as a compile-time constant form and as a weak function returning true, used to force an unconditional halt path.
